source.title: The Anatomy of Implicit Bias: Information Allocation in Neural Network Training
source.authors: Gong-Yue Zhang; Zhi-Yong Wang; Dong-Han Liu; Wei-Hong Ren; Yi-Xuan Sheng; Hong-Hai Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how training factors relate to training and test losses and allocation measures, using its own experiments and diagnostics. It does not reproduce the specific interventions or measurements in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on the preconditioning exponent p, batch size, data statistics, width, activation, schedules, and related allocation measures. The p comparisons bear on adaptive optimization and test performance, but do not compare Adam with SGD or test the other versions' specific claims. No result tests memorization of random labels, interpolation-threshold widening, convolutional versus fully connected generalization, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The CIFAR-100 experiments compare p=0, which removes second-moment preconditioning and gives a momentum-like update, with positive p adaptive updates under the same training recipe. Their held-out performance bears on V4, although the study does not compare standard Adam directly with standard SGD. The synthetic matched-progress probes do not test the benchmark-specific versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors propose training-time information allocation as a complementary view of implicit bias, report distinct allocation signatures across training factors, identify a CIFAR-100 median–tail trade-off, and report small accuracy gains or faster convergence from dynamic p schedules on facial-expression tasks. They do not conclude that smaller p universally generalizes better.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a continuous preconditioning-exponent probe and allocation diagnostics, rather than the original versions' memorization, interpolation, architecture comparison, optimizer comparison, batch-budget, dropout, sharpness, or example-removal recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Preconditioning exponent p changes channel-gain and update ratios; batch size changes gain and update ratios in different directions; data preset, width, activation, learning-rate setting, and schedule also change reported measures. In CIFAR-100, the p-associated tail effect is more pronounced at learning rate 0.1.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic matched-progress comparisons retain strong p-dependent internal allocation differences while external test-loss quantiles nearly coincide.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive preconditioning can change internal signal allocation without materially changing matched-progress external losses.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning-rate differences largely collapse after matching training progress.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate effects in this synthetic task primarily reflect training progress.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch size changes gain and update ratios in opposite directions while matched-progress test p95 remains similar.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size can change internal allocation without a corresponding matched-progress tail-loss penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: Data presets and width change test outcomes and gradient allocation at similar training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data statistics and model width affect allocation and generalization at matched empirical loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing p alters the identity of high-loss training examples.

record.problems: The controlled source-map task is synthetic, and the paper describes the weight–bias grouping as a minimal projection. Numerical uncertainty estimates are not stated. Some results are summarized from figures without precise values. The CIFAR-100 p sweep does not isolate a simple optimizer-versus-optimizer comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results were omitted. The study's schedule table and facial-expression recognition results concern an allocation-aware training method and its performance; they do not directly test a listed version's claim about generalization gaps or the specific interventions in those versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization with the same recipe, and chance-level held-out performance on random labels.
Test error after widening beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.

Standard Adam versus standard SGD; full-strength p=0.5 versus p=0 on image benchmarks; systematic optimizer-specific tuning; broader tuning, weight-decay recovery, optimizer switching, and language-model outcomes.
Large-batch penalties under fixed epoch budgets and their removal through longer training or recipe changes.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Influence-based memorization estimates and retraining after removing memorized versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The record overlooks the relevant p=0 control: the paper explicitly defines it as removing second-moment scaling. This permits a qualified V4 test using partial adaptive updates, without equating the experiment with a standard Adam-versus-SGD benchmark. The improved test median is not evidence against worse aggregate held-out performance. No uncertainty estimates establish the statistical reliability of the reported differences.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label held-out accuracy.
Widening beyond the zero-training-error threshold and its effect on test error. The width probe reports results at matched training loss near 0.5.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization; local connectivity and learned sparse connections.
Comparisons of Adam or other adaptive methods against SGD or momentum SGD; broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, optimizer switching, and language-model results.
Large versus small batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets, and whether longer training or recipe changes remove a batch penalty.
Dropout versus no dropout, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing high-influence memorized examples and comparing against random-example removal.

rows.baseline: p=0: test-loss p95 near 0.90; p99 near 1.0
rows.value: From p=0 to p=0.5, test-loss p95 stays near 0.90 and p99 near 1.0.
rows.note: Authors say external test-loss quantiles almost collapse after matching training progress; this compares degrees of preconditioning, not adaptive optimizers against SGD.
rows.check: The reported collapse is accurate, but this synthetic task does not test V4's image-classification or language-benchmark comparison. 'Absent' incorrectly treats it as an absence of V4's effect.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared test-loss distribution and accuracy across fixed preconditioning exponent p settings.
rows.measure: test median loss; test p95 loss; proportion of test samples with loss larger than 5; accuracy
rows.note: Across p values the median loss falls while the high-loss tail rises; held-out accuracy does not improve monotonically.
rows.check: For V4, use p=0 as the nonadaptive baseline, rather than p=-0.4. At p=0, accuracy is 78.66% and mean test loss is 0.859; at p=0.1, 0.2, and 0.3, accuracy is 77.87%, 77.79%, and 77.09%, and mean loss is 0.889, 0.947, and 1.110. Positive preconditioning worsens aggregate held-out performance despite improving median loss. Negative-p comparisons do not themselves establish V4.

rows.subject: ResNet-18

rows.note: The text says the median–tail trade-off is more pronounced under the larger learning rate.
rows.check: For V4, use p=0 as the nonadaptive baseline. At p=0, accuracy is 78.69% and mean test loss is 0.863; at p=0.1, 0.2, and 0.3, accuracy is 77.28%, 76.23%, and 75.28%, and mean loss is 0.973, 1.195, and 1.401. The original negative-p baseline obscures the relevant comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-18

rows.note: The text says similar results occur under η=0.1, but does not give exact values there.
rows.check: Hard-sample overlap measures sample identity, not memorization influence or the accuracy effect of removing examples required by V8.
